```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, dpi = 96
)
card_url <- "https://github.com/sportsdataverse/hoopR-mbb-data/blob/main/docs/models/ratings.md"
# the ratings release is parquet-only, so the loader needs arrow
has_arrow <- requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE)
```

**A team that wins by 20 against the weakest schedule in the country has not shown what a team that wins by 20 against the strongest has.** Opponent-adjusted efficiency ratings correct for that: each team's offense is measured against the defenses it faced, and its defense against the offenses. `load_mbb_ratings()` returns the SportsDataverse's adjusted ratings for every men's college team and season since 2006, in the spirit of KenPom and Bart Torvik's T-Rank. This article explains what the ratings estimate, how they are computed and checked, and how to use them.

The official model card is [ratings.md](`r card_url`) in the `hoopR-mbb-data` repository. Numbers below are computed in this article from the published release unless labeled "as reported in the model card".

## What does the dataset contain?

One row per team and season:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `adj_o` | Adjusted offensive efficiency: points scored per 100 possessions against an average defense. |
| `adj_d` | Adjusted defensive efficiency: points allowed per 100 possessions against an average offense. Lower is better. |
| `adj_em` | Adjusted efficiency margin, `adj_o - adj_d`: points per 100 possessions better than an average team. |
| `adj_tempo` | Adjusted possessions per 40 minutes. |
| `raw_o`, `raw_d` | Unadjusted points scored and allowed per 100 possessions. |
| `games`, `rank`, `adj_em_z` | Games played, national rank by `adj_em`, and `adj_em` as a z-score within the season. |

`team_id` is the ESPN team id, the same key as `load_mbb_team_box()` and `load_mbb_schedule()`.

## How are the ratings computed?

As described in the model card, the engine is an iterative opponent adjustment: a fixed-point solve, on the efficiency-margin scale, over the season's game matrix. In outline, a solver of this kind works like this:

1. Start from each team's raw offensive and defensive efficiency in every game (points per 100 possessions).
2. Adjust each game's offensive efficiency for the opponent's current defensive rating, and vice versa, relative to the league average.
3. Average the adjusted game values into new team ratings, and repeat until the ratings stop changing (the fixed point).

Tempo is adjusted the same way. The "features" are the game results themselves and the attribution is the published offense/defense split; there is no hidden model to explain. Ratings are recomputed from scratch on every run, so corrections to the underlying play-by-play and box scores flow through automatically.

## Loading and exploring the ratings

```{r load, eval = has_arrow}
library(hoopR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

ratings <- load_mbb_ratings(seasons = 2006:2026) |>
  mutate(team_id = as.character(team_id))

team_names <- load_mbb_team_box(seasons = 2026) |>
  distinct(team_id = as.character(team_id), team = team_display_name)

ratings |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    teams = n(),
    teams_10plus_games = sum(games >= 10),
    mean_adj_em_all = round(mean(adj_em, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    mean_adj_em_core = round(mean(adj_em[games >= 10], na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  ) |>
  tail(8)
```

The full frame includes every opponent any Division I team played, including non-Division I teams with one or two games, which pulls the overall mean far below zero. The **core** (teams with 10 or more games) sits near zero, as an average-relative scale should.

### Raw versus adjusted

```{r raw_vs_adjusted, eval = has_arrow, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of raw efficiency margin against adjusted efficiency margin for 2025-26 men's college basketball teams with at least 10 games."}
core_2026 <- ratings |>
  filter(season == 2026, games >= 10) |>
  mutate(raw_em = raw_o - raw_d) |>
  left_join(team_names, by = "team_id")

c(
  core_teams = nrow(core_2026),
  cor_adj_em_raw_em = round(cor(core_2026$adj_em, core_2026$raw_em), 3),
  cor_adj_em_z = round(cor(core_2026$adj_em, core_2026$adj_em_z), 3)
)

ggplot(core_2026, aes(raw_em, adj_em)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#2C3D50") +
  labs(
    title = "Schedule strength separates raw and adjusted margin",
    subtitle = "2025-26, teams with 10+ games; dashed line is adjusted = raw",
    x = "Raw efficiency margin (per 100 possessions)",
    y = "Adjusted efficiency margin (adj_em)",
    caption = "Data: hoopR::load_mbb_ratings()"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Teams above the dashed line played schedules tougher than average and are rated better than their raw margin; teams below it padded their numbers against weak opponents.

## How are the ratings checked?

### The level gate

A rank correlation against another rating system (Spearman's rho) cannot see a scale error: multiply every rating by 100 and the ranks do not move. So, as described in the model card, the publish path carries an **absolute level gate** beside the engine's rank checks. Over the core teams (10+ games, applied once 150 teams qualify), each season's mean `adj_o`, `adj_d`, `adj_em`, `adj_tempo` and the standard deviation of `adj_em` must sit inside fixed bands, and no rating may be missing or infinite. Here it is re-run on the assets the loader returns:

```{r level_gate, eval = has_arrow}
bands <- list(adj_o = c(95, 118), adj_d = c(95, 118), adj_em = c(-8, 8),
              adj_tempo = c(60, 76), sd_adj_em = c(10, 22))

gate <- ratings |>
  filter(games >= 10) |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    core_teams = n(),
    non_finite = sum(!is.finite(adj_em) | !is.finite(adj_o) | !is.finite(adj_d)),
    mean_adj_o = mean(adj_o), mean_adj_d = mean(adj_d), mean_adj_em = mean(adj_em),
    mean_adj_tempo = mean(adj_tempo), sd_adj_em = sd(adj_em)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pass = core_teams < 150 | (
      non_finite == 0 &
        between(mean_adj_o, bands$adj_o[1], bands$adj_o[2]) &
        between(mean_adj_d, bands$adj_d[1], bands$adj_d[2]) &
        between(mean_adj_em, bands$adj_em[1], bands$adj_em[2]) &
        between(mean_adj_tempo, bands$adj_tempo[1], bands$adj_tempo[2]) &
        between(sd_adj_em, bands$sd_adj_em[1], bands$sd_adj_em[2])
    )
  )

gate |>
  mutate(across(starts_with(c("mean", "sd")), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

```{r gate_summary, include = FALSE, eval = has_arrow}
n_pass <- sum(gate$pass, na.rm = TRUE)
n_seasons <- nrow(gate)
```

`r if (has_arrow) paste0(n_pass, " of ", n_seasons, " published seasons pass the gate on the current release.") else ""` The model card notes that an earlier 2011 asset failed to converge (every rating missing), which is exactly the failure the finiteness check refuses; the table above reflects whatever the release holds today. The bands catch the errors a rank check misses: a per-game instead of per-100 scale divides every level by about 1.5, and a sign flip mirrors `adj_em`.

### Program stickiness

Programs persist even when rosters do not, so a team's rating should carry over strongly from one season to the next:

```{r stickiness, eval = has_arrow}
ratings |>
  filter(games >= 10) |>
  select(team_id, season, adj_em) |>
  inner_join(ratings |> filter(games >= 10) |>
               transmute(team_id, season = season - 1, adj_em_next = adj_em),
             by = c("team_id", "season")) |>
  filter(is.finite(adj_em), is.finite(adj_em_next)) |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(teams = n(), yoy_r = round(cor(adj_em, adj_em_next), 3)) |>
  tail(8)
```

### How much of a game margin does the rating explain?

An in-sample illustration: for 2025-26 games between two core teams, compare the final margin with the difference in adjusted margins, scaled to the game's possessions. The ratings were computed from these same games, so this is a description of fit, not a forecast test.

```{r game_fit, eval = has_arrow}
games_2026 <- load_mbb_team_box(seasons = 2026) |>
  filter(team_home_away == "home") |>
  transmute(home_id = as.character(team_id), away_id = as.character(opponent_team_id),
            margin = team_score - opponent_team_score)

fit_df <- games_2026 |>
  inner_join(core_2026 |> select(home_id = team_id, home_em = adj_em, home_t = adj_tempo), by = "home_id") |>
  inner_join(core_2026 |> select(away_id = team_id, away_em = adj_em, away_t = adj_tempo), by = "away_id") |>
  mutate(expected = (home_em - away_em) * ((home_t + away_t) / 2) / 100)

fit <- lm(margin ~ expected, data = fit_df)
c(games = nrow(fit_df), r_squared = round(summary(fit)$r.squared, 3),
  home_edge_points = round(unname(coef(fit)[1]), 2))
```

The intercept is the average home edge in points left over once team strength is accounted for (neutral-site games are included as "home" games here, which shrinks it slightly).

## Who was best in 2025-26?

```{r top25, eval = has_arrow}
ratings |>
  filter(season == 2026) |>
  left_join(team_names, by = "team_id") |>
  arrange(rank) |>
  select(rank, team, adj_o, adj_d, adj_em, adj_tempo, games) |>
  mutate(across(adj_o:adj_tempo, \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  head(25) |>
  print(n = 25)
```

## Limitations

- **Early-season ratings start flat.** There is no preseason prior yet, so ratings in November rest on a handful of games.
- **Home court, travel and altitude** are not modeled beyond what the game results imply.
- **Non-Division I opponents** appear with very few games and extreme ratings; filter on `games` (10+ is a good default) before ranking or averaging.
- **External agreement is checked where the engine is trained.** The model card describes rank gates against KenPom- and Torvik-class references in the engine's own repository; the level gate above is the scale check at publish time.
